sentences.text: In January 2026, a gallon of regular gas cost well under its average for Joe Biden's presidency.
By spring, it cost well over it.
So is gas cheaper now than under Biden? That depends on what you mean by now.
President Trump made the case at a cabinet meeting: "It was $4 and $5 for a gallon of gas", he said, "and now it's probably 225".
By this spring, CBS News was reporting pump prices "at their highest point since mid-2022".
Here is the record to check them against: the Energy Information Administration's national monthly average for regular gas, in dollars not adjusted for inflation.
From February 2021 through January 2025, it came to $3.46 a gallon, with a peak of $4.93 in June 2022.
In 2025 the lowest month, December, came to $2.89, well above the president's guess.
Every month of 2025 was below the Biden-era average, but about level with the last months of his term.
Then the weekly price jumped, from $3.02 in the first week of March 2026 to $4.50 by mid-May.

News reports tied the jump to the war with Iran: MS NOW said gas was "up by well over a dollar since the war started", and NBC News put it plainly: "it's the war in Iran that's largely causing fuel prices to rise".
West Texas Intermediate crude oil jumped in the same month, from $64.51 a barrel in February to $91.38 in March.
Those reports tie the rise to the war; the price record shows when prices jumped, but on its own it cannot rule out other causes.
In October, President Trump made the same kind of claim about crude: "Oil was higher under Biden than it is under Trump".
In September, the latest month in the EIA's crude table, it averaged $97 a barrel, higher than in every month of Biden's term except March through July 2022.
Gas, meanwhile, averaged $4.36 a gallon in September.
Put the lines side by side and the pump price has moved with crude under both presidents: both peaked in June 2022, both ended 2025 lower than they started it, and both jumped in March 2026.
That fits what a guest on PBS NewsHour said, that the pump price "is set in a global market"; but prices moving together cannot show that policy played no part, since policy can move crude itself.
So whether gas is cheaper than under Biden depends on the month: yes, against his term's average, through February 2026; no, in every month since March, though still short of that 2022 peak.
But gas is one price among many. What about prices overall?
The channel Squirrelly Economics put the comparison this way: "Prices rose about 21% over Biden's 4 years".
The Bureau of Labor Statistics' consumer price index agrees: it rose 21.4 percent from January 2021 to January 2025.
From January 2025 to September 2026, the latest month, it rose 6.1 percent.
But that sets a full term against one still under way, over a much shorter stretch.
Over stretches as long as this one so far, at each end of Biden's term, prices rose 13.5 percent at the start, January 2021 to September 2022, and 4.5 percent at the end, May 2023 to January 2025.
And the count is still running: the year-on-year rate climbed from 2.4 percent in February 2026 to 3.7 percent in September, the same months gas jumped.

So prices have risen more slowly this term than across Biden's term as a whole, though faster than in his last stretch, and by a smaller margin than the totals suggest; and the index cannot say how much of either rise any president caused.
Both answers turned on the calendar: which month counts as now, and how long a stretch you measure.
So when someone tells you prices are lower, ask: compared with when, and over how long?
And when the pump price moves, check what crude oil did that month.
